power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Introduction: Peripheral neural injuries, known as polyneuropathy, are largely described in patients with Type-2 Diabetes Mellitus (T 2 DM).
However, less is known about the T 2 DM- associated cerebral White Matter (WM) integrity.
Previous studies highlighted mediating effects of inflammation in the T 2 DM-brain association.
It is, however, still unclear whether   Interleukin-6 (IL-6) mediates specifically T 2 DM-cerebral WM integrity.
Brain Study: Health Disparities (HABS-HD) study.
Diffusion-weighted scans were analyzed, and diffusion parameters were averaged in major WM tracts.
Effect sizes (Cohen's d) were calculated after adjusting for relevant confounders.
Mediation analysis was performed using 1000-fold non-parametric bootstrapping of 95% confidence intervals (CI).
The results were adjusted for multiple testing using the False Discovery Rate method (FDR).
Results: Several WM tracts showed significant impairment in T 2 DM participants after adjusting for confounders and multiple testing (posterior thalamic radiation (adj.
Cohen's d=0.14[0.03-024]), anterior corona radiata (adj.
Cohen's d=0.15[0.04-0.26]), cingulum (adj.
Cohen's d=0.14[0.03-0.25]), inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (adj.
Cohen's d=0.16[0.06-0.27]), genu of the corpus callosum (adj.
Cohen's d=0.13[0.03-0.24]), and body of the corpus callosum (adj.
Within two years, the effect sizes showed an increasing trend.
Even in cognitively unimpaired participants, T 2 DM was associated with locally reduced WM integrity.
IL-6 statistically mediated up to 15% of these major associations.
Conclusions: The study demonstrated T 2 DM-associated impairment of intracerebral WM integrity.
In T 2 DM, microstructural WM changes might start before clinically objectified cognitive impairment.
The role of systemic inflammation needs to be assessed in causal frameworks.
The main hypothesis of the study is that participants with T 2 DM have impaired WM integrity compared to those without T 2 DM.
The second hypothesis is that IL-6 plays a mediating role in this association.

The aim of the current study was to explore the association between diffusion tensor imaging (DTI)-measured WM integrity biomarkers and T 2 DM in community-dwelling middle- aged and older US adults with equally represented ethnic groups and to understand the statistical mediating role of IL-6 in this constellation.
The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines were followed for the elaboration of this manuscript.
The study population is a subset of the Health and Aging Brain Study: Health Disparities

Differences in participants with and without T 2 DM were assessed using the Wilcoxon rank sum test, Pearson's Chi-squared test, Then, a detailed matrix showing only significant correlation coefficients was created in both subpopulations to quantitatively estimate an indirect biomarker of WM connectivity in each group.
Linearity assumptions were tested for all models where the FA of WM tracts was the outcome, T 2 DM was the predictor, and all covariates were included.
Model-based adjusted means were computed using the Estimated Marginal Means method.
The difference in adjusted mean FAs between participants without and with T 2 DM was computed by subtraction (non-T 2 DM minus T 2 DM).
A model-based adjusted effect size (Cohen's d) was then derived from the results.
To ensure the correctness and comparability of the findings, a standardized regression coefficient (ß) was also reported.
The confounders included in Cohen's d and standardized regression coefficient equations are detailed in 2.6.
Significant results were adjusted for multiple testing using the false discovery rate (FDR) method in order to reduce Type I error risk.
All p-values resulting from different tract comparisons (Adjusted p-value*) were included in the same FDR equation (n=16; Adjusted p FDR -value).
The significant results defined the " T 2 DM-specific WM tracts" for this study.
The first sensitivity analysis was based on assessing differences between non-T 2 DM and T 2 DM regarding WM FAs across all tracts at 2-year follow-up using the same earlier described method.
Then a second sensitivity analysis was performed on cognitively unimpaired participants at baseline.
The association between T 2 DM and WM integrity in "T 2 DM-specific WM tracts" was assessed using a multivariable linear regression analysis, including the pre-described confounders (2.6.).

A confounder-adjusted non-parametric mediation analysis with 1000fold bootstrapping of a 95% confidence interval (CI) was performed on significant associations in order to assess the mediating role of IL-6.
Results were calculated as the proportion of mediated effect on the total effect and presented as percentages (%) with 95% CI.

text.text: Only a few studies explored the association between IL-6 and DTI biomarkers.
These included a limited number of patients and showed conflicting results.

While some did not find any significant association between IL-6, FA, and mean diffusivity (MD) in a general biethnic population, (36) another study showed significant regional associations between higher IL-6, impaired FA, and radial diffusivity (RD) in schizophrenia patients, but not healthy controls. (37) In a larger sample of participants, there were no genetically explainable correlations between IL-6 levels and DTI parameters on WM microstructures. (33) Our study showed lower FA in T 2 DM participants compared to the control group.

(42, 43) Later studies showed that even in physiological conditions, high or increasing levels of inflammatory biomarkers in early adulthood predict impaired WM structures in later ages. (44) The association between IL-6 levels and WM integrity might start during the conceptional stage.

WM integrity, T 2 DM, and alternative diagnostic methods Diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI) might provide additional information on T 2 DM-related WM integrity than DTI-specific parameters.
Mean kurtosis (MK) values were more sensitive to negative changes associated with T 2 DM disease duration in the genu of the corpus callosum and anterior corona radiata.

(51) Although our DTI-based analysis revealed anatomically plausible results, advanced methods such as DKI and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) might provide additional information.

Clinical implications Metabolic syndrome -including dyslipidemia and obesity -(52) and modifiable lifestyle habits -including sedentary behavior and smoking -are well-recognized risk factors for peripheral diabetic polyneuropathy (53) and mental health adversities and vice versa.
(54) Clinical interventions targeting glucose regulation showed a major role in preventing intracerebral complications.
(55) These hypotheses need to be explored in larger randomized controlled trials focusing specifically on WM integrity.
Intensive lifestyle interventions in randomized controlled studies showed beneficial effects in preventing diabetic polyneuropathy.
(56) These results might reflect similar preventive effects on intracerebral levels and need to be assessed in longitudinal interventional studies with a special focus on T 2 DM and brain health.

This hypothesis is also supported by a Danish population-based study where a decline in diabetic distal symmetrical polyneuropathy incidence in recent years was probably associated with improved medical care.

(57) Shortterm interventions also showed that physical activity improves the cardiovascular autonomic function in T 2 DM patients, (58) a further potential actor in the interrelation between diabetes and intracerebral WM integrity.

Despite well-monitored T 2 DM, the risk of peripheral diabetic neuropathy tends to increase with the years, (59, 60) and higher triglyceride levels might present a concomitant risk factor that needs to be taken into account in the preventive strategies.
(59, 61) However, another study showed that an aggressive lowering of plasma cholesterol levels presents a risk factor for diabetic polyneuropathy.
(62) Clinicians need to balance the benefits and risks of T 2 DM- specific and lipid-lowering therapies for better brain health and WM integrity, as well.
(63) Initial nerve alterations might be reversible to a certain degree in well-controlled new-onset T 2 DM.

(60) For later stages of the disease, a randomized controlled trial showed that intravenous immunoglobulin therapy did not improve the demyelinated peripheral polyneuropathic features in T 2 DM patients.
(64) This should motivate early interventional strategies to prevent irreversible complications.

Behavioral inflammation-lowering interventions in younger ages (Mediterranean diet, regular physical activity, stress prevention, and mental health support…) might present further strategies to mitigate the T 2 DM-associated inflammatory risks on brain health and, particularly, WM integrity.
Peripheral diabetic polyneuropathy is a largely explored pathology, whereas less is known about the involvement of low-grade inflammation in the cerebral WM integrity associated with T 2 DM.
This is mainly due to the lack of direct tools to assess WM integrity. dMRI measures are surrogate biomarkers of WM integrity based on water molecule diffusivity.
Thus, they provided strong anatomical correlates and are largely used in neuroimaging studies.
Second, the cerebral involvement in T 2 DM has so far been less explored, and very little is known about the T 2 DM-brain crosstalk.
Such a knowledge gap highlights the novelty of the current study in this evolving area.
This is the first study to assess the association between T 2 DM and DTI-related WM integrity with a prospective design, while taking into account the mediating role of IL-6.
The high number of participants with equally represented multiethnic backgrounds and with complete biological and neuroimaging data is a major strength of the current study.

The study included community-dwelling participants, which might expose the data to selection bias of socially active individuals, and the findings might not be replicated in those with restricted social networks, limited mobility, and poor physical conditions.

The study population tends to have an average of a good educational level, and most of the participants with T 2 DM are under at least one form of medication, which does not reflect the findings in less compliant ones and those suffering from severe diabetes complications.
Furthermore, the results do not represent potential findings in patients with T 1 DM, who   were not eligible for the source cohort.
The presented analyses and results do not conclude any causal inference owing to the observational nature of the data.
Longitudinal and experimental research is needed to confirm these relationships.
The study demonstrated T 2 DM-associated impairment of intracerebral WM integrity.
As in previous studies, IL-6 seems to play a statistical mediating role in this relationship, partly explaining the observed effects.
Its predictive value at early stages of T 2 DM-WM impairment needs to be explored in future studies in order to ensure early preventive interventions.
